reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: NIST defines the recovery time objective (RTO) as the overall length of time an information system's components can be in the recovery phase before negatively affecting the organization's mission or business processes. This exercise starts the clock at the moment of disruption; some plans start it at the disaster declaration, and the plan must say which.
Derivation: 45 + 30 + 120 = 195 minutes (3 hours 15 minutes), which is within the 240-minute RTO with 45 minutes of margin.

Independent check: 240 − 195 = 45 minutes of margin. A test that timed only restore and validation measured 120 of the 195 minutes; the 75 minutes of detection and decision were assumed, not observed.

Misconception to reject: 'a two-hour restore test proves a four-hour RTO.' The objective covers the whole recovery as the plan defines it, and an untimed detection or escalation step can consume the margin without anyone noticing until a real event.
Change one factor: data growth slows the restore to 3 hours while the other steps stay the same. The total becomes 45 + 30 + 180 = 255 minutes, missing the RTO by 15 minutes.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: NIST defines the recovery point objective (RPO) as the point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage. Here backups complete at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00, each is assumed to be restorable, and no other copy of the data exists.

Derivation: the worst case is a failure just before the next backup. A failure at 11:59 restores to the 06:00 backup and loses 5 hours 59 minutes of data, which approaches the full 6-hour interval and far exceeds the 1-hour RPO.

Independent check: for periodic backups the worst-case loss equals the backup interval plus any delay before a backup becomes usable. With a 6-hour interval and no delay the bound is 6 hours, consistent with the 11:59 example.

Misconception to reject: 'the RPO is how quickly we restore.' Restore speed is governed by the RTO; the RPO concerns how old the recovered data may be. A fast restore of a 6-hour-old backup still misses a 1-hour RPO.
Change one factor: take snapshots every 30 minutes. The worst-case loss falls to 30 minutes, within the 1-hour RPO, provided each snapshot is complete and restorable.

Source and limits: the RPO definition follows NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-34r1. A backup that fails a restore test provides no recovery point, so schedule restore tests as well as backups.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: a plan makes five claims: (a) the on-call engineer is reached within 15 minutes; (b) the failover decision is made within 30 minutes; (c) the database is restored within 120 minutes; (d) the application is validated within 30 minutes; (e) customers are notified with an approved template. The figures are invented.

Derivation: a tabletop exercise is discussion-based; it can show that roles and decisions are understood (b, e) but does not time technical work. A timed restore test measured (c) at 110 minutes and (d) at 25 minutes, both within their claims.

Independent tally: of five claims, two have measured timing evidence (c, d), two have discussion evidence only (b, e) and one (a) is untested, so it remains an assumption until a paging drill measures it.
Misconception to reject: 'we tested the plan' after a tabletop alone. Discussion exercises build shared understanding; they do not show that systems can be recovered or how long recovery takes.

Change one factor: run an unannounced paging drill. If the on-call engineer responds in 22 minutes, claim (a) is falsified by 7 minutes; update the roster or the claim instead of averaging the result with earlier, faster ones.

Source and limits: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 treats testing, training and exercises as part of maintaining a contingency plan: https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-34r1. A single successful test is evidence for that run's conditions, not a guarantee for every scenario.

vocabulary.term: Incident Leadership: Create Clarity Under Pressure
vocabulary.definition: During a major incident, leadership is the work of establishing roles, priorities, communication, and decision cadence so technical responders can solve the problem.
A recovery point objective defines the targeted point in time to which data should be recovered after a disruption, expressing tolerated data loss.
A recovery time objective defines the maximum targeted duration for restoring a system or service after disruption.
